mechanisms.conditioning_logic: Condition on the cross-team pairing: Team A's shots-FOR (16.0 all-prior, 14.6 recent) against Team B's shots-on-target-AGAINST (4.156 all-prior, 6.2 recent), AND Team B's shots-FOR (10.442 all-prior, 9.2 recent) against Team A's shots-on-target-AGAINST (3.312 all-prior, 3.8 recent). The asymmetry is that Team A produces far more shots but Team B allows more shots-on-target per match than Team A does. Measure whether the combined on-target output in matches where one side has a large shots-volume advantage but the other side has a higher shots-on-target-allowed rate diverges from the competition baseline.
mechanisms.expected_relationship_to_test: Total match shots-on-target rises when the high-volume shooting team faces a high shots-on-target-allowed opponent, but the relationship is asymmetric: the high-volume side's on-target count rises more steeply than the low-volume side's, producing a skewed distribution of on-target activity between the two teams rather than a symmetric uplift.
mechanisms.mechanism_statement: Team A generates substantially more shots and shots-on-target than Team B, while Team B concedes shots-on-target at a higher rate than Team A concedes. The joint relationship between one team's shot-production volume and the opponent's shots-on-target-allowed rate — across both sides simultaneously — conditions the match's total on-target activity in a way that neither team's own shot mirror alone captures.
mechanisms.why_not_baseline_equivalent: This requires jointly conditioning on two distinct observables (shots volume FOR one team, shots-on-target AGAINST the other team) for both sides simultaneously. It is not reducible to a single observable mirror or a single observable with one coarse band; it is an asymmetric cross-team, cross-observable relationship.

mechanisms.conditioning_logic: Condition jointly on Team A's possession-FOR (~60%) and Team A's corners-FOR (6.36 all-prior, 5.2 recent) alongside Team B's possession-FOR (~53%) and Team B's corners-FOR (5.61 all-prior, 4.0 recent). The mechanism tests whether, in matches where one team holds a large possession advantage over the other (not just over a league baseline), the possession-to-corner conversion ratio for the dominant side is higher than for the subordinate side — i.e., whether the relationship between possession share and corner generation is non-linear or asymmetric across the two sides of the same match.
mechanisms.expected_relationship_to_test: The team with the larger possession advantage in a given match generates corners at a disproportionately higher rate relative to its possession share than the lower-possession team, suggesting a non-linear or threshold relationship between possession dominance and corner production.
mechanisms.mechanism_statement: Team A holds dominant possession (~60%) and generates far more corners (6.36 all-prior) than Team B (5.61 all-prior), while Team B concedes fewer corners (4.60) than Team A concedes (3.90). The joint relationship between possession dominance and corner-kick generation — across both teams — tests whether the possession-to-corners conversion rate differs between the dominant-possession side and the lower-possession side in the same match.
mechanisms.why_not_baseline_equivalent: This jointly conditions on two distinct observables (possession and corner_kicks) for both teams simultaneously, testing a cross-observable ratio relationship. It is not a single-observable mirror or a single-band split; it requires measuring the possession-to-corners conversion rate as a function of the possession gap between the two sides.

mechanisms.conditioning_logic: Condition jointly on each team's fouls-FOR and yellow_cards-FOR across all prior matches. Compute the yellow-cards-per-foul ratio for each team and test whether the team with the higher absolute foul rate (Team B) also has a disproportionately higher yellow-card-per-foul ratio, or whether the relationship saturates. Additionally, test whether the asymmetry in foul profiles (Team A low-foul, Team B high-foul) predicts a divergence in yellow card totals beyond what each team's yellow card average alone would suggest.
mechanisms.expected_relationship_to_test: Yellow cards per foul rise with total foul volume in a non-linear (threshold/saturation) manner: teams committing more fouls accumulate yellow cards at a disproportionately higher rate per foul, and the asymmetry between the two teams' foul profiles amplifies the difference in their yellow card totals beyond a simple additive expectation.
mechanisms.mechanism_statement: Team A commits far fewer fouls (9.17 all-prior) than Team B (13.69 all-prior), while Team B concedes fewer fouls (11.97) than Team A concedes (14.13). This creates a strongly asymmetric foul-committing profile between the two sides. The joint relationship between each team's foul rate and its yellow-card rate tests whether the team that commits fewer fouls (Team A, 1.62 YC/match) accumulates yellow cards at a lower rate per foul than the team that commits more fouls (Team B, 2.26 YC/match), and whether this ratio diverges from competition norms.
mechanisms.why_not_baseline_equivalent: This jointly conditions on two distinct observables (fouls and yellow_cards) and tests a ratio/non-linear relationship between them, not a simple mirror of either observable alone. The asymmetry across the two teams adds a second dimension that cannot be captured by a single-observable band split.

mechanisms.conditioning_logic: Condition on the within-match half split: compare each team's first-half corner rate to its second-half corner rate (both FOR and AGAINST), and test whether the match-level first-half share of total corners is elevated when Team A (first-half concentrated) hosts Team B (flat distribution). This requires half-level resolution and the joint conditioning on both halves' corner counts for both teams simultaneously — not just a single half's average.
mechanisms.expected_relationship_to_test: When a first-half-concentrated corner producer (Team A) faces a team with a flat half-distribution (Team B), the first half accounts for a larger share of total match corners than the competition baseline, with the concentration effect driven primarily by the home team's first-half production rather than a symmetric uplift across both halves.
mechanisms.mechanism_statement: Team A produces corners heavily in the first half (3.41 FH vs 2.93 SH all-prior) while Team B's corner production is more evenly split (2.83 FH vs 2.77 SH). The within-match half-level distribution of corner production differs between the two teams. This tests whether the team with a first-half corner concentration advantage (Team A) generates a disproportionate share of total match corners in the first half when facing a team with a flatter half-distribution (Team B), and whether this half-concentration pattern is stable or regresses.
mechanisms.why_not_baseline_equivalent: This requires half-level data resolution and conditions on the within-match temporal distribution (first-half vs second-half ratio) of a single observable for both teams simultaneously. It is not a simple single-observable split by one coarse band; it tests a within-match sequencing/regime structure across two halves jointly for both sides.

mechanisms.conditioning_logic: Condition jointly on both teams' half-level goal-FOR and goal-AGAINST rates. Specifically: Team A's second-half scoring rate (1.14) combined with Team B's second-half conceding rate (0.77) versus Team A's first-half scoring rate (0.90) combined with Team B's first-half conceding rate (0.64). Test whether the second-half goal concentration is amplified when both the scoring team's second-half production advantage AND the conceding team's second-half defensive vulnerability align in the same direction — a two-dimensional half-level conditioning that cannot be reduced to either team's half split alone.
mechanisms.expected_relationship_to_test: The second-half share of total match goals is elevated beyond competition norms when the attacking team has a second-half scoring concentration AND the defending team has a second-half conceding concentration, with the effect stronger than either team's half-split pattern would predict in isolation.
mechanisms.mechanism_statement: Team A scores more goals in the second half (1.14 SH vs 0.90 FH all-prior) while conceding more in the second half (0.53 SH vs 0.43 FH). Team B scores more in the first half relative to its second half (0.53 FH vs 0.69 SH all-prior) and concedes more in the second half (0.77 SH vs 0.64 FH). The cross-team asymmetry in half-level goal-scoring and goal-conceding profiles — where Team A is a second-half scorer facing a team that also concedes more in the second half — tests whether the combined second-half goal rate in this specific matchup exceeds the first-half rate by more than competition norms would predict.
mechanisms.why_not_baseline_equivalent: This conditions simultaneously on two teams' half-level goal profiles (FOR and AGAINST) across both halves, requiring half-level data resolution and a joint two-team, two-observable-period conditioning. It is not reducible to a single team's half split or a single observable with one coarse band.
